newsitem.title: MALDIVES: South Asian nations settle festering dispute.
newsitem.headline: South Asian nations settle festering dispute.

text.p: Seven South Asian nations have patched over a disagreement that had threatened to divide the fledgling economic bloc into two groups led by arch-foes India and Pakistan, diplomats said on Sunday.

Foreign ministers of the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) resolved the dispute over regional sub-groupings ahead of a meeting in the Maldives of the bloc's heads of government set to start on Monday.

The dispute arose in April when India and three smaller neighbours -- Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal --agreed to set up a smaller group to cooperate in water-sharing, the environment, transport and trade.

Pakistan, and to a lesser extent Sri Lanka and the Maldives, objected, saying the Growth Quadrangle sub-group was at odds with the spirit of the 12-year-old SAARC, which wants to set up a regional free trade area by 2005.
Islamabad saw the Growth Quadrangle as an attempt by its bigger neighbour India to isolate Pakistan.

"Pakistan at this point in time is extremely apprehensive that it will be left out, partly because you will find the formation of non-Saarc groupings emerging," said Samina Ahmed, a research analyst at Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies.
"This is being looked here as an attempt to subvert SAARC."
But India said the four nations in the sub-regional group shared problems, particularly in the areas of water resources and transport, which could be addressed by special projects.
The festering dispute had threatened to sour the ninth SAARC summit.

But diplomats said SAARC foreign ministers agreed at the weekend that member countries could cooperate in smaller groups provided the agreements applied to specific projects and did not undermine SAARC.
"It has been agreed that under the SAARC charter, some member countries can cooperate with each other but remaining within the SAARC," a senior Pakistani diplomat said.
"Bilateral or even quadrilateral projects don't weaken SAARC, provided they are specific projects," an Indian diplomat said.
SAARC was launched in 1985 in Dhaka with the goal of accelerating economic growth in the region, which has 1.2 billion people, over 500 million of whom live in poverty.
